title: Europe’s summer heat exposed a gap between cheap daytime power and evening supply
summary: Christine Lagarde sees a modest, mostly temporary effect of the summer’s extreme weather on aggregate euro area activity, alongside potentially lasting losses where damage is concentrated. Her argument turns on timing. River traffic can resume when water levels recover. Farming income, regional productive capacity and uninsured wealth can take much longer to recover. Electricity provides a second example. More low-carbon generation reduced exposure to expensive gas early in 2026, yet there was still a shortage of power at the hours when households needed cooling most. The ECB President makes a case for insurance, grids and storage. The article offers no new policy-rate decision or rate-path guidance.

The contrast between aggregate output and local damage is already visible. Lagarde cites more than 30,000 excess deaths across Europe during the heatwaves and 400,000 hectares burned in Spain and France. Low water on the Rhine disrupted German transport, but ECB staff expected most of the effect on GDP growth to unwind with normal flows. In Italy heat and drought weighed on output. The French and Spanish losses had so far concentrated in agriculture, forestry and tourism. Historical regional estimates put activity 1.5% lower two years after a heatwave and 3% lower four years after a drought. Those estimates describe different events, geographies and horizons. They cannot be added or applied directly to euro area GDP. Lower productivity and relocation can depress local activity even when production elsewhere holds up. Poorer agricultural supply could also lift food inflation in the coming year.

Lagarde highlights a balance-sheet channel. Nearly three quarters of euro area businesses are heavily dependent on at least one service provided by nature, with water-related services most exposed. Separately, nearly 12% of euro area output is exposed to risks from inadequate flood protection. Neither statistic measures an expected financial loss. Historically insurance has covered only about a quarter of European catastrophe losses, leaving households and firms to finance rebuilding or seek public assistance. Fiscal authorities may face constraints when claims arrive together. Lagarde supports advancing an ECB–EIOPA proposal for EU-level public-private reinsurance through the Commission’s resilience framework. The article does not specify attachment points, premiums or how losses would ultimately be shared.

The interaction of weather with the Middle East energy shock matters for interpreting electricity prices. In Spain, gas plants set the electricity price in around 80% of hours in the first nine months of 2020, against just over 20% in the corresponding period of 2026. This measures hours of marginal price-setting, not gas’s share of annual generation. Low-carbon supply helped wholesale power prices respond less to higher gas prices than in 2021–22. During heatwaves, cooling demand rose just as drought constrained hydro generation and limited cooling water for nuclear plants. Solar was the only major source that performed better than usual in these episodes, but its output fell in the evening while cooling demand stayed high. Average generation shares conceal the hours when a marginal unit is most valuable.

The Commission aims to double electricity’s share of final energy consumption by 2040. Lagarde argues that achieving the economic benefit requires moving power across space through grids and across hours through storage. She cites estimates of over €2 of other system costs saved per euro invested in grid upgrades. A system-wide saving does not reveal which utility or storage operator earns it. With new connections taking two to ten years, she proposes common rules for quicker connection of firms with on-site generation or storage in return for helping the grid during stress. Much of the investment would require private financing. In her view deeper European capital markets and predictable climate policy, including carbon pricing, would lower financing costs. The terms on which firms would provide capacity and recover their investment remain open.

questions.question: Which evening hours determine the value of storage or a flexible connection?
questions.detail: Spain’s gas price-setting frequency fell substantially across the first nine months, but the heat left a narrower evening shortage. Compare hourly day-ahead and balancing prices, generation by technology, demand, cross-border flows and storage availability in the system operators’ summer records. A battery’s achievable net revenue depends on the spread it can capture, its duration and its connection, even when the system-wide gain is large.

questions.question: Who ultimately funds reconstruction in the most exposed regions?
questions.detail: The historical coverage ratio indicates a large protection gap. It does not allocate this summer’s losses among households, firms, insurers and governments. Consult regional loss assessments, insurance claims and policy terms alongside fiscal commitments and the cited reinsurance proposal. Their timing matters for cash needs and for distinguishing impaired borrower collateral from a temporary financing gap.

questions.question: How much of the disruption survives the next growing season?
questions.detail: Staff expect the immediate German transport effect largely to reverse, while Lagarde identifies a risk to food prices over the coming year. Track river freight volumes separately from regional crop yields, farm-gate prices, import substitution and retail food prices. Official agricultural and regional output releases could distinguish a harvest loss with persistent price effects from a short-lived transport bottleneck.
